conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: CorrectionLengthAtLeastHalfTrendDuration
candidates.quote: After a bear channel that lasted 20 or 30 bars, the correction was likely to have at least half as many bars as a general rule.
candidates.description: After a trend leg that lasted N bars, do not expect the countertrend correction to be complete (and a resumption/second-leg entry to be high probability) until the correction itself has lasted at least a fraction F of N bars.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a timing filter on when a continuation setup is trusted, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: needs a swing/leg detector to know when the prior trend leg started and ended, plus a persistent bar counter for the correction; the comparison itself is a trivial ratio once those counts exist

notes: Brooks gives 'about half' as a general rule, not an exact fraction; 0.5 is a reading of the text.

This chapter is heavy with worked chart examples that reuse pattern vocabulary already mined elsewhere in this book: two-bar reversal (01_example_of_how_to_trade_a_reversal.json V01), wedge/three-pushes (00_front_matter.json, 01-part_i..., 05_wedges...), trend-channel-line overshoot (00_front_matter.json V00, 01-part_i..., 02_signs..., 04_climactic...), always-in flips (15_always_in.json), moving-average gap bars (00_front_matter.json, 01_example...), double top/bottom flags (01_example_of_how_to_trade_a_reversal.json), H1/H2 leg counting (00_front_matter.json High1Leg/High2Leg), failed breakouts (09_failures.json, 18_patterns_related_to_yesterday_breakouts.json), final flags (01-part_i... FinalFlagReversalSetup), doji/inside/outside bars (00_front_matter.json), and trend-line breaks (01_example..., 03_major_trend_reversal.json). None of those are redefined here; only genuinely new statements from this chapter are recorded below.

candidates.name: BreakevenExitAtOriginalEntryAfterScaling
candidates.quote: This is the area where some started to scale in, and once the market gets back to their very first entry, they often exit their entire position.
candidates.description: For a position built by scaling in at progressively better prices during an adverse move, exit the entire position once price returns to the level of the original (first) entry, roughly breakeven on the earliest, worst-priced fill.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (an exit at a remembered price level rather than a stop order)

complexity.reason: position-history read of the entry price; if the engine's ctx.EntryPrice() reports the position's average price rather than the very first scaled-in fill, this is only an approximation of the book's 'first entry' level

notes: Brooks describes this as trader behavior ('they often exit'), not a strict rule, and it presumes a scaled entry with a known first fill; kept because it is a concrete, mechanizable exit idea distinct from the peak-profit-giveback family already in rules/CATALOG.md (ProfitProtector, TrailingStop) and from 01-part_i...'s PartialProfitAtPriorSwingTestWithPauseBar, which exits at a chart level rather than at the trader's own entry price.

candidates.name: AvoidEntryNearSessionClose
candidates.quote: The day was over and there was not enough time left for the bears to make a profit, so they therefore chose to not short into the close.
candidates.description: Do not initiate a new intraday entry once the session clock is within X minutes of the close; there is not enough remaining time for a typical trade to reach a profit target.

complexity.reason: a single comparison against the bar's close time; the book gives no exact minute threshold so one is invented

notes: Distinct from rules/CATALOG.md's TimeWindow (a fixed HHMM..HHMM band) in that the threshold here is relative to the session's own close, not an absolute clock time; TimeWindow can approximate it if the session close time is fixed and known in advance.
Possibly related to reference/brooks/mined/reversals/11_key_times_of_the_day.json's FinalHourTrendContinuationNoPullbackEntry (not read in full here); the dedup pass should compare the two.

candidates.name: ExitLongOnOpposingLow2SetupUnlessTrendReversed
candidates.quote: Countertrend traders trying to buy in a bear trend should always exit on a low 2 signal, unless the trend has clearly already reversed and the low 2 setup is likely to fail.
candidates.description: Exit an open countertrend long that was bought against a bear trend as soon as a low-2 short setup (a second consecutive attempt to break below the recent swing low) forms, since that is a strong resumption signal for the bears.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (an exit gated by a counting setup rather than a fixed offset)

complexity.reason: depends on a Low2/High2 pullback-attempt counter (swing-pivot tracking of successive failed breakout attempts), plus the book's own escape clause ('unless the trend has clearly already reversed') is pure discretion and is dropped here

notes: The book's own low2/high2 (H1/H2/L1/L2) counting family is defined elsewhere in this book's mined output as the High1Leg/High2Leg pair in 00_front_matter.json; no Low1/Low2 twin was found there as of this mining pass, so low2ShortSetupTrue is left as an undefined helper for the authoring pass to wire up once that primitive exists.

The 'unless the trend has clearly already reversed' qualifier is discretionary judgment with no bar-level test and is intentionally simplified away; this is a lossy but still useful approximation of the book's rule.
Overlaps conceptually with 15_always_in.json's ExitOnOppositeSignalWeakerThanReversal; the dedup pass should compare.

chapter_summary: Chapter 21 is a worked-examples chapter: five annotated intraday charts (T-Note, EUR/USD, soybeans, crude oil, two 1-minute Emini scalp charts) narrated bar-by-bar using the pattern vocabulary built up across the rest of the book (two-bar reversals, wedges/three pushes, trend-channel-line overshoots, always-in flips, moving-average gap bars, double tops/bottoms, H1/H2/L1/L2 counting, failed breakouts, final flags, ii setups, trend-line breaks). Almost none of that vocabulary is new to this chapter, so this file only records the handful of genuinely new, generalizable statements the chapter adds on top: a correction-length-vs-trend-length heuristic, a breakeven exit tied to a trader's own original entry price after scaling in, a filter against opening new trades too close to the session close, and an explicit exit-the-countertrend-long-on-an-opposing-low-2-setup rule. Everything else is narration applying already-mined primitives to specific, unreproduced chart bars and was rejected as redundant or purely discretionary.
